ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study protocol was approved by the local ethical committees from the enrolled centres: School of Dentistry of the University of São Paulo (FOUSP), Federal University of Santa Catarina (UFSC), Rio de Janeiro State University (UERJ) and Iguaçu University (UNIG), under the approval number 42602820.0.1001.0121.

The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the local ethical committees from the enrolled centres: the Schools of Dentistry of the Universidade de São Paulo (USP), Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina (UFSC), Universidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro (UERJ) and Universidade Iguaçu (UNIG), under the approval number 42602820.0.1001.0121.
Design: 199 primary molars from children aged 3-9 years were randomised to the CTZ or ZOE groups.

In addition, the study protocol was prospectively registered in ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT04942158) and published elsewhere. 21 Children were enrolled in the study only after providing written assent or, if they could not read or write, verbal assent, and after their legal guardians signed an informed consent form.
table.formatted: In addition, the study protocol was prospectively registered in ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT04942158) and published elsewhere. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> Children were enrolled in the study only after providing written assent or, if they could not read or write, verbal assent, and after their legal guardians signed an informed consent form.

table.text: Participants were recruited between October 2021 and March 2023 and were subsequently followed for 24 months after treatment.

Participants were initially recruited from four study centres; however, one centre did not complete the study due to challenges with recruitment and participant recall, resulting in the loss of all enrolled participants from that centre (n = 20).
Thus, 156 of the 199 randomised participants completed the 24-month follow-up (76 in the ZOE and 80 in the CTZ).
All parents or legal guardians of the participants signed an informed consent form, and the participants signed an assent form.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The sample size was calculated using the Sealed Envelope® estimator (https://www.sealedenvelope.com/power/binary-noninferior/). An initial sample of 114 participants was calculated, assuming a success rate of 92%, a non-inferiority margin of 15%, a significance level of 5%, and 90% power. Adding 20% considering possible losses of followup and 60% due to the multicentre design (20% to each additional centre), the required sample size was 218 participants (109 in each group). This sample size was revised on two occasions due to slower-than-anticipated participant recruitment and the discontinuation of one study centre. Following these adjustments, the minimum required sample size was recalculated as 182 participants (91 per group).

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/qwen3.5:4b' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. Some essential information could not be detected: effect_size, effect_size_metric ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "unknown", statistical_test = "other", sample_size = 218, alpha_level = 0.05, power = 0.9, effect_size = NA_real_, effect_size_metric = NA_character_, software = "other"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "The sample size was calculated using the Sealed Envelope® estimator (https://www.sealedenvelope.com/power/binary-noninferior/). An initial sample of 114 participants was calculated, assuming a success rate of 92%, a non-inferiority margin of 15%, a significance level of 5%, and 90% power. Adding 20% considering possible losses of followup and 60% due to the multicentre design (20% to each additional centre), the required sample size was 218 participants (109 in each group). This sample size was revised on two occasions due to slower-than-anticipated participant recruitment and the discontinuation of one study centre. Following these adjustments, the minimum required sample size was recalculated as 182 participants (91 per group)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

table.formatted: Results: Overall success rates in the ITT population were 64.3% for CTZ and 58.7% for ZOE, with a difference of 5.6% (95% CI: -9.3 to 20.4; p<0.01).

table.formatted: Children's behaviour, immediate discomfort and postoperative pain were similar between groups (p>0.05).
table.expanded: Children's behaviour, immediate discomfort and postoperative pain were similar between groups (p>0.05).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < 0.05", "p<0.01", "p<0.01", 
"p>0.05"), Text = c("The main analysis followed the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle, comparing success proportions with the Miettinen-Nurminen method, considering a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 15% (p < 0.05).", 
"Results: Overall success rates in the ITT population were 64.3% for CTZ and 58.7% for ZOE, with a difference of 5.6% (95% CI: -9.3 to 20.4; p<0.01).", 
"Mean; standard deviation clinical time was significantly shorter in CTZ (36.3; 9.8 min) than in ZOE (63.0; 16.3 min) (p<0.01).", 
"Children's behaviour, immediate discomfort and postoperative pain were similar between groups (p>0.05)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.formatted: Children's behaviour, immediate discomfort and postoperative pain were similar between groups (p>0.05).
table.expanded: Children's behaviour, immediate discomfort and postoperative pain were similar between groups (p>0.05).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p>0.05", Sentence = "Children's behaviour, immediate discomfort and postoperative pain were similar between groups (p>0.05)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::
